issues.legal_issue: A later statute that adopts an earlier acquisition law with substantial adaptations incorporates that law rather than merely referring to it, so later amendments to the earlier law do not ordinarily apply automatically.
material_facts: The town-improvement statutes adopted the general acquisition law subject to numerous and substantial modifications.
The statutes had their own schemes and procedures for improvement and acquisition, and their schedules adapted acquisition-law provisions to those schemes.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition law, as modified, was incorporated into each of the three State statutes; subsequent amendments to the acquisition law did not ordinarily affect acquisitions under those statutes.
issues.legal_principle: Whether provisions are incorporated or merely referred to depends on statutory construction, including the language and context of the later statute. On incorporation, the adopted provisions become part of the later statute, and later amendments to the earlier statute do not ordinarily carry across. The Court relied on Secretary of State v. Hindustan Cooperative Insurance Society Ltd.; U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad v. Jainul Islam; and State of Madhya Pradesh v. M.V. Narasimhan, which identifies exceptions where the statutes are supplemental or in pari materia, the later statute would otherwise be unworkable, or the amendment expressly or by necessary intendment applies. The Court rejected the contrary view in Bhatinda Improvement Trust v. Balwant Singh.

predicates.town_improvement_acquisition: The proceeding concerns a compulsory acquisition for a town-improvement scheme under a separate local enactment.
predicates.earlier_law_adopted_with_substantial_mod: The local enactment adopts an existing acquisition law while making substantial adaptations to its provisions.
predicates.local_acquisition_scheme_exists: The local enactment provides its own scheme and procedure for carrying out improvements and acquiring land.

issues.definition: When a town-improvement acquisition proceeds under a local enactment that substantially adapts an adopted acquisition law and supplies its own acquisition scheme, later changes to the adopted law do not automatically apply.

issues.legal_issue: Later amendments concerning the determination and payment of compensation apply to acquisitions under the town-improvement statutes where excluding them would produce arbitrary and hostile discrimination.
material_facts: The local statutes used the acquisition law, as adapted, for compulsory acquisitions and provided compensation rules that could differ from those applying to acquisitions under the general law.
The statutes also permitted land to be obtained through routes other than compulsory acquisition under the adopted law.

Excluding later compensation amendments for compulsory acquisitions would leave owners with less compensation than owners whose land was acquired under the general law, without a relevant distinction from the owners’ perspective.
issues.conclusion: The claimants were entitled, where applicable, to the compensation benefits introduced by the 1984 amendments, including the additional amount, solatium, and interest provided for by the amended compensation provisions.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Article 14 of the Constitution and the principle that equally situated owners cannot receive different compensation merely because land is acquired by a different authority or under a different acquisition route. It relied on Nagpur Improvement Trust v. Vithal Rao and U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad v. Jainul Islam, and on the constitutional-avoidance principle stated in Kedar Nath Singh v. State of Bihar. It distinguished acquisitions under the town-planning provisions considered in Prakash Amichand Shah v. State of Gujarat, where the general acquisition law did not apply.

predicates.town_improvement_acquisition: The proceeding concerns compulsory acquisition under a town-improvement enactment that adopts the general acquisition law.
predicates.compensation_rules_differ_by_acquisition: The compensation available for the acquisition differs from that available to owners whose land is acquired under the general acquisition law.
predicates.no_relevant_owner_distinction: The different acquisition route or acquiring authority does not create a relevant difference between the affected landowners.
predicates.conforming_compensation_construction_is_: The local enactment can be read to apply the later compensation benefits without contradicting its text.

issues.definition: Where compulsory acquisitions under a town-improvement enactment would otherwise pay less to owners who are not relevantly different, and the enactment can be read consistently to avoid that disparity, the later compensation benefits apply.

issues.legal_issue: A later amendment imposing a time limit for making the declaration step in the general acquisition process does not apply to acquisitions under the town-improvement statutes after the acquisition law has been incorporated into those statutes.
material_facts: The relevant notices initiating the acquisitions were followed by declaration-equivalent notices more than three years later.
The challenged acquisitions proceeded under the Nagpur and Uttar Pradesh town-improvement enactments.
The time limit relied on had been added to the general acquisition law after the local enactments were made.
issues.conclusion: The later time-limit amendment did not govern the acquisitions, and the declaration-equivalent notices were not invalid merely because they were issued more than three years after the initiating notices.
issues.legal_principle: As the acquisition law had been incorporated into the local enactments, later amendments to it did not ordinarily affect acquisitions under those enactments. The Court applied the incorporation principles in U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad v. Jainul Islam and State of Madhya Pradesh v. M.V. Narasimhan.

predicates.town_improvement_acquisition: The proceeding concerns compulsory acquisition under a town-improvement enactment that adopts the general acquisition law.
predicates.declaration_step_follows_initiating_noti: The local acquisition process uses a later declaration-equivalent step after an initiating notice.
predicates.relied_on_time_limit_was_added_after_loc: The asserted deadline was introduced into the general acquisition law after the local enactment was made.

issues.definition: A declaration-equivalent step in a town-improvement acquisition is not invalid under a deadline added to the general acquisition law after the local enactment was made.

issues.legal_issue: The additional compensation introduced by the 1984 amendment is unavailable where the acquisition award was made before the applicable transitional threshold.
material_facts: The relevant awards were made before the transitional threshold specified for entitlement to the additional compensation.
The High Court had granted the additional compensation in some appeals despite those awards having been made before that threshold.
issues.conclusion: The claimants whose awards were made before the transitional threshold were not entitled to the additional compensation, and the contrary directions were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the five-judge decision in K.S. Paripoornan v. State of Kerala, which overruled Union of India v. Zora Singh and held that entitlement to the additional amount for earlier acquisition proceedings is restricted by the transitional provisions of the amending law.

predicates.acquisition_compensation_claim: The proceeding seeks the additional compensation introduced by an amendment to the general acquisition law.
predicates.award_made_before_transitional_threshold: The acquisition award was made before the transitional threshold relevant to entitlement to the additional compensation.

issues.definition: A claim for the additional compensation fails when the acquisition award was made before the applicable transitional threshold.

issues.legal_issue: Interest is payable on the compensation amounts awarded under each of the three compensation sub-sections, including the additional amount and solatium.
material_facts: The claimants sought interest on the additional amount payable under the compensation provision.
The controlling larger-bench decision had held that the total compensation includes the amounts payable under all three compensation sub-sections.
issues.conclusion: The claimants were entitled to interest on the amount payable under the additional-compensation sub-section, as well as on the other compensation components.
issues.legal_principle: The Court followed Sunder v. Union of India, which held that the compensation amount on which interest is payable includes the amounts determined under all three sub-sections of the compensation provision. It also referred to Prem Nath Kapur v. National Fertilizers Corporation of India Ltd., whose contrary treatment of interest on the additional amount was superseded by the larger-bench ruling in Sunder.

predicates.acquisition_compensation_claim: The proceeding concerns compensation awarded for an acquisition under the general acquisition law.
predicates.compensation_includes_statutory_addition: The awarded compensation includes statutory additions to the basic market-value amount, such as an additional amount or solatium.

issues.definition: When acquisition compensation includes statutory additions, interest is payable on all components of the compensation award.

issues.legal_issue: The government, rather than the local improvement trust, is the acquiring authority when compulsory acquisition proceeds through the statutory process adopted by the town-improvement enactments.
material_facts: Each local enactment provided for land acquired through the statutory acquisition process to be transferred to the trust after the cost of acquisition was paid.
The claim that the trust itself was the acquiring authority was advanced to distinguish the compensation-equality principle based on the identity of the acquiring body.
issues.conclusion: The government is the acquiring authority under that compulsory-acquisition process, and in any event the identity of the acquiring body does not justify different compensation for otherwise equally situated owners.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on Om Prakash v. State of Uttar Pradesh, which interpreted a materially similar provision requiring the collector to transfer acquired land to a local body after payment of acquisition costs. It also applied Nagpur Improvement Trust v. Vithal Rao, which held that compensation cannot differ merely because land is acquired for or by a different authority.

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_for_local_body: The proceeding uses a statutory compulsory-acquisition process to obtain land for a local public body.
predicates.land_transferred_after_acquisition_costs: The statutory process requires the land to be transferred to the local body after the acquisition costs are paid.

issues.definition: When land is compulsorily acquired for a local body and transferred to it after acquisition costs are paid, the government is the acquiring authority.
